clauses.reason: Terminated by its own terms at the close of Tuesday, December 31, 1957, the second of the two days on which it excuses employees for one-half day (the first is Tuesday, December 24, 1957). The order sets no later date and no continuing rule; the exclusion paragraph only limits the excusal. Recorded as 1957-12-31, inclusive; the exclusive reading (the end when December 31 begins) is the alternative. Actor: the order itself. The dossier holds no own-terms record for this order, so the end cites the order's own operative clause, which contains the stated days. No later amending event is held; Executive Order 10358 (1952) is cited by the order for its holiday definition and is earlier, not a later event.

research_rationale:
Identity: the registered original is the Federal Register printing of Executive Order 10744 (22 FR 10001, PDF pages 1-1; Federal Register issue of December 13, 1957; govinfo PDF text layer held at jobs/fr-originals/data/full_run/texts/EO_10744.txt), headed Executive Order 10744, signed by Dwight D. Eisenhower on December 10, 1957. The census register gives the same number, date and subject (Excusing Federal Employees From Duty for One-Half Day on December 24, and One-Half Day on December 31, 1957). The text is an official scan read through its machine text layer; I read it for OCR damage and note below where damage matters. Inventory: the dossier's single whole-order clause covers both paragraphs of the order. The first paragraph excuses covered employees from duty for one-half day on each of two stated days, Tuesday, December 24, 1957, and Tuesday, December 31, 1957, and treats each such half-day as a holiday for the purposes of Executive Order 10358 of June 9, 1952 and of the statutes on compensation and leave, with exceptions for employees excluded by agency heads or whose absence would be inconsistent with law. The second paragraph says the order does not excuse employees whose posts of duty are required for national security or other public reasons in the judgment of their agency heads. Own terms: the last stated day is December 31, 1957, so the order's own terms end it then; I record the end inclusive at the close of that day, with the exclusive reading (the end when that day begins) as the alternative. The three chosen machine searches (U.S. Code through 2026-10-09, eCFR as of 2026-10-14, Office of the Federal Register disposition notes plus operative sentences of 17521 saved order texts) each state their coverage with no warning; their coverage notes were read. They search by this order's number, and the one later-events hit is Executive Order 10358, an earlier order (1952) that this order itself cites for its holiday definition, so it is not a later change to this order.

savings.reason: The order contains no savings, exception or transitional clause beyond the national-security exclusion in its second paragraph, which limits the excusal and does not continue it; I read the whole text. Pay and leave for the excused half-days rest on the compensation and leave statutes, for which the order treats each half-day as a holiday; those effects are completed and do not keep the order operative after December 31, 1957.
